newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq wants chief U.N. arms envoy to open new page.
newsitem.headline: Iraq wants chief U.N. arms envoy to open new page.

text.p: Iraq wants newly appointed United Nations arms inspector Richard Butler to open a new page with Baghdad, the ruling Baath party newspaper al-Thawra said on Monday.

The official Iraqi News Agency INA said Butler, an Australian who took over as chairman of the United Nations Special Commission (UNSCOM) on Iraq this month, arrived in Baghdad for talks with officials.
INA gave no further details. Butler replaced Sweden's Rolf Ekeus, who built up UNSCOM in 1991.

Al-Thawra said Iraq would cooperate with UNSCOM -- a Security Council affiliate entrused with ensuring Iraq complies with the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire resolution by dismantling its weapons of mass destruction.
"...What Iraq sincerely wants and seeks is that the Special Commission with its new chairman opens a new page with it," al-Thawra said in a front-page editorial.
"It is in the interest of Iraq that its ties with the Special Commission are stable and it is confirmed that Iraq will cooperate with it," Thawra said.

Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein warned on Thursday in a speech marking the July 17 revolution that Iraq's ties with the United Nations could reach a deadlock if the Security Council did not lift the sanctions imposed on Baghdad for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
Thawra harshly attacked Butler's predecessor Rolf Ekeus and blamed last month's standoff between the commission and Iraq on him and the United States.

"Ekeus, upon directions from it (U.S.), intended to create a crisis between Iraq and the Special Commission. He deliberately launched inspections of Iraqi sites of security and sovereignty nature," the newspaper said.

Last month Iraq barred U.N. inspectors from entering three sensitive sites, prompting the Security Council to issue a resolution warning Iraq it would face further sanctions if it blocked U.N. inspectors.

The daily al-Jumhouriya assailed the council's decision and accused France, Russia and China, which are adopting a less stringent policy against Iraq from that of the United States and Britain, of doing nothing to block that resolution.
It urged these countries to set up an "arbitration committee to examine and decide on differences between Iraq and the (U.N. inspection) teams."

UNSCOM must certify that Iraq has no weapons of mass destruction before the United Nations can lift curbs on Iraqi oil exports, although Baghdad is allowed limited oil exports under a humanitarian deal.
Richard Butler, the U.N. official in charge of scrapping Iraq's weapons of mass destruction, headed for Baghdad on Monday for talks with Iraqi officials, a United Nations spokesman said.
